Blocks and tackle. The power obtained by this contrivance is calculated as follows: Divide the weight by double the number of pulleys in the lower block; the quotient is the power required to balance the weight.

— Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements (1908), no. 14

text:
C. R. Otis’s safety-stop for the platform of a hoisting apparatus. A are the stationary uprights, and B is the upper part of the platform working between them. The rope, a, by which the platform is hoisted, is attached by a pin, b, and spring, c, and the pin is connected by two elbow levers with two pawls, d, which work in ratchets secured to the uprights, A. The weight of the platform and the tension of the rope keep the pawls out of gear from the ratchets in hoisting or lowering the platform, but in case of the breakage of rope the spring, c, presses down the pin, b, and the attached ends of the levers, and so presses the pawls into the ratchets and stops the descent of the platform.

— Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements (1908), no. 278
provenance: Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements, 21st edition (1908), movement 278; public-domain excerpt. Transcription: https://507movements.com/mm_278.html.

Tongs for lifting stones, etc. The pull on the shackle which connects the two links causes the latter so to act on the upper arms of the tongs as to make their points press themselves against or into the stone. The greater the weight the harder the tongs bite.

— Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements (1908), no. 494
